extracted.intended_audience: covered entities and their contractors (health insurers, issuers, plan sponsors, third party administrators, pharmacy benefit managers), health care providers, legal and compliance officers, and advocates engaged in section 1557 compliance
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and interpretive standards for applying HHS OCR's final rule implementing section 1557 nondiscrimination obligations across health programs, benefit design, provider networks, medical diagnostic equipment, and related affiliates/contractors. Includes examples, scope rules, and enforcement approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third party administrator liability for discriminatory plan design
rubrics_metrics.description: If a third party administrator is a covered entity under section 1557, it is responsible for ensuring that its actions do not discriminate on the basis of race, color, national origin, sex, age, or disability; where a covered third party administrator plays a role in designing benefits for self-insured group health plan coverage, it must not do so in a manner that results in discrimination on a prohibited basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Third party administrators cannot avoid liability simply because a plan sponsor requested a discriminatory design; e.g., designing a plan that excluded enrollees of a certain race would violate section 1557 and the designer (the third party administrator) would be liable notwithstanding the sponsor's request.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pharmacy benefit manager (PBM) coverage and liability
rubrics_metrics.description: Pharmacy benefit managers are health programs or activities and are covered under the rule if they receive Federal financial assistance or if they are part of the operations of a recipient principally engaged in provision/administration of health-related services or coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A PBM that is subject to section 1557 (by receiving federal funds or as part of principally engaged operations) has liability similar to a covered third party administrator. OCR will evaluate whether responsibility for the challenged action lies with the PBM or the plan sponsor when investigating complaints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between administrative tasks and benefit design activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative actions such as developing documents or preparing policy booklets for clients, alone, do not constitute third party administrator liability for discriminatory plan design features if the third party administrator merely relays information consistent with underlying plan terms it played no role in developing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liability hinges on whether the entity played a role in developing or designing plan terms versus merely communicating or implementing them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liability for outsourcing and subcontractors
rubrics_metrics.description: A covered entity that outsources the implementation or benefit design of discriminatory plans remains liable under this rule for any discriminatory plan terms; covered entities are responsible for the conduct of their subcontractors and cannot contract away civil rights obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A third-party company that develops or manages discriminatory plans on behalf of a covered entity is only itself liable under section 1557 to the extent it is a recipient or subrecipient of Federal financial assistance or part of a principally engaged recipient's operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affiliate/subsidiary coverage—case-by-case analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether liability under section 1557 extends across affiliated companies is determined by a fact-specific case-by-case analysis, not automatic coverage solely due to relationship to a federally funded entity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR will examine degree of interrelatedness, common ownership and control, and whether legal separation was intended to avoid liability. A legal entity 'truly independent' of an issuer's federally funded activities is unlikely to be covered; longstanding civil rights case-law principles inform the analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stop-loss insurance treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Stop-loss insurance, which provides coverage for the benefit of employers/plan sponsors (not individuals), does not implicate the rule where it does not discriminate against individuals on protected grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR will consider whether stop-loss mechanisms target or penalize individuals (e.g., people with disabilities) in ways that result in discrimination; if stop-loss does not discriminate against individuals, it does not fall within this rule's prohibitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious employer and exemption interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 1557 does not apply to an employer or plan sponsor with regard to its employment practices, including provision of employee health benefits; covered entities subject to section 1557 may seek religious exemptions consistent with §92.302(b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious employers may obtain coverage/administration from entities not subject to section 1557; covered entities remain prohibited from discriminating in provision or administration of coverage even if employer requests products aligning with religious beliefs, subject to available regulatory exemptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Network design as a form of benefit design (network adequacy enforcement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provider networks are encompassed within the term 'benefit design' and OCR will accept and investigate complaints related to provider networks as possible discriminatory benefit designs under section 1557.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR will not set minimum network adequacy standards in this rulemaking, but will investigate on a case-by-case basis whether network designs exclude individuals or deny them benefits based on protected characteristics; analyses will be fact-intensive and consider neutrality of rules applied and potential pretextual reasons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of potentially discriminatory network practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Network design practices that commenters characterized as discriminatory include: low reimbursement rates that lead to lower provider participation, arbitrary limits to in-network providers, limiting participation of safety-net providers, insufficient providers with accessible medical equipment, narrow pharmacy networks, and performance requirements related to cost or other outcome/quality measures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR acknowledges these examples as potentially discriminatory; if such practices have the effect of dissuading enrollees with high health needs from enrolling or denying access, they may violate section 1557 and will be investigated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Excessive administrative burden as discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Plan designs that subject individuals protected by section 1557 to excessive administrative burdens to access coverage benefits that other enrollees do not have to navigate may be discriminatory under section 1557.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR notes problems like opaque or arbitrary appeals processes and 'phantom networks' (providers listed as in-network but not accepting patients) as evidence of administrative structures that can disparately impact protected groups; such burdens will factor into investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for nondiscriminatory network development
rubrics_metrics.description: Covered entities must develop their networks in a nondiscriminatory manner, consistent with existing State and Federal network adequacy and other laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When OCR determines a network design is discriminatory, covered entities are expected to provide neutral, nondiscriminatory reasons for the design that are not pretextual. OCR will defer to and coordinate with other agencies/standards that set minimum network adequacy requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: No creation of uniform federal minimum network adequacy standards here
rubrics_metrics.description: OCR will not establish minimum network adequacy standards in this rulemaking because many network adequacy standards are governed by other Departmental regulations and state laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR's enforcement focuses on nondiscrimination under section 1557 rather than establishing uniform time/distance or provider-mix standards; other agencies (e.g., CMS, states) set and enforce those technical standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical Diagnostic Equipment (MDE) accessibility obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: Denial of services to individuals with disabilities due to inaccessible MDE can constitute discrimination under section 1557, the ADA, and section 504; providers must make their health programs and activities accessible to individuals with disabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR did not adopt the U.S. Access Board's MDE Standards in this rulemaking, but emphasizes that acquisition of accessible MDE and staff training on its use are necessary for meaningful access; inaccessible MDE contributes to poorer health outcomes and may trigger enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and scope of MDE standards (policy position)
rubrics_metrics.description: OCR will not require covered entities in this rule to meet the Access Board's MDE Standards or set federal timelines for replacing older equipment in this rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR is pursuing separate rulemaking under section 504 to adopt enforceable MDE standards; in absence of enforceable standards, OCR will continue to enforce existing nondiscrimination obligations and consider provider training and practical use of equipment in investigations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on requiring patients to bring personal aides for transfers
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal civil rights laws (section 504, title II of the ADA, and section 1557 implementing regulation) forbid providers from requiring patients with disabilities to bring someone with them to appointments to assist with transfers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patients who have been required to bring another person to an appointment for transfers are encouraged to file complaints with OCR; providers must provide reasonable accommodations and accessible equipment instead of imposing such requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessible MDE as reasonable modification or alternative
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing accessible MDE is one method to ensure access for patients with disabilities and may constitute a reasonable modification under disability rights laws; in specific situations offering transportation to another facility with accessible MDE may be appropriate but is less preferable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR prefers on-site acquisition and use of accessible MDE; where on-site access is not feasible, temporary measures (like transportation) may be considered in context, but cannot replace obligation to provide accessible programs and services generally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration requirement covers practices risking institutionalization or segregation
rubrics_metrics.description: The integration requirement in §92.207 has been clarified to extend to practices that result in the serious risk of institutionalization or segregation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This change underscores that benefit designs or network practices leading to segregation or institutionalization of people with disabilities can violate the nondiscrimination and integration prohibitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on coverage denials and pretextual medical management
rubrics_metrics.description: §92.207(c) now prohibits 'denying or limiting coverage of the health service or determining that such health service fails to meet applicable coverage requirements including reasonable medical management techniques such as medical necessity requirements' when such denial or limitation is based on unlawful animus, bias, or is a pretext for discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covered entities may use legitimate medical necessity and management criteria, but such decisions must not be discriminatory or amount to pretext for unlawful bias; OCR will review whether denials are based on neutral medical criteria or discriminatory intent/effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on sex discrimination related to marital, parental, or family status (§92.208)
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining whether an individual satisfies any policy or criterion regarding access to its health programs or activities, a covered entity must not take an individual's sex into account in applying any rule concerning an individual's current, perceived, potential, or past marital, parental, or family status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provision bars policies that treat individuals differently on the basis of sex when applying rules tied to marital/parental/family status (e.g., assigning a male spouse as guarantor when a female spouse receives services but not vice versa). It does not prohibit distinctions based on marital status alone (e.g., married vs. unmarried) unless those distinctions are applied differently by sex.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection of same-sex couples and family structures under §92.208
rubrics_metrics.description: Benefits and coverage that are offered to married different-sex couples (e.g., fertility treatments) must be offered in a nondiscriminatory manner to married same-sex couples; policies that impose standards (e.g., definitions of 'infertility') that effectively deny coverage to same-sex couples on sex-related bases may violate section 1557.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OCR recognizes documented harms to same-sex couples (e.g., visitation, medical decision-making) and treats sex-based differential application of marital/family rules as sex discrimination; related forms of association discrimination are addressed in §92.209.
